items.back: $f$ has a local max at $p$ if $f(q)≤f(p)$ for all $q$ in some neighborhood of $p$.
$f^{(n)}=(f^{(n−1)})'$. Existence of $f^{(n)}(x)$ requires $f^{(n−1)}$ to exist near $x$.
For $f:[a,b]→ℝ^{k}$, $f'(x)$ is the vector $y$ with $|(f(t)−f(x))/(t−x)−y|→0$; equivalently, differentiate each component.
If $f'(x)$ exists then $f$ is continuous at $x$.
If $f$ has a local max or min at $x∈(a,b)$ and $f'(x)$ exists, then $f'(x)=0$.
If $f,g$ are continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, some $x∈(a,b)$ has $[f(b)−f(a)]g'(x)=[g(b)−g(a)]f'(x)$.
If $f$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and $λ$ lies between $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$, then $f'(x)=λ$ for some $x∈(a,b)$. Corollary: a derivative has no simple (jump) discontinuities.
items.note: Derivatives need not be continuous, but they satisfy the IVT.

items.back: If $f,g$ are differentiable on $(a,b)$, $g'≠0$, $f'/g'→A$ as $x→a$, and either $f,g→0$ or $g→±∞$, then $f/g→A$.

If $f^{(n−1)}$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $f^{(n)}$ exists on $(a,b)$, then for $α≠β$ in $[a,b]$, $f(β)=P(β)+\dfrac{f^{(n)}(x)}{n!}(β−α)^{n}$ for some $x$ between them, where $P$ is the degree $n−1$ Taylor polynomial at $α$.

items.front: MVT fails for complex/vector functions; inequality survives
items.back: For $f:[a,b]→ℝ^{k}$ continuous and differentiable on $(a,b)$: $|f(b)−f(a)| ≤ (b−a)|f'(x)|$ for some $x$.

items.modelProof: At a local max $x$, the difference quotient is $≥0$ for $t<x$ and $≤0$ for $t>x$ (near $x$). The limit is both $≥0$ and $≤0$.
Let $h(t)=[f(b)−f(a)]g(t)−[g(b)−g(a)]f(t)$. Then $h(a)=h(b)$. $h$ attains a max or min in the interior (or is constant), where $h'=0$ by 5.8. Take $g(t)=t$ for the ordinary MVT.
Say $f'(a)<λ<f'(b)$. Let $g(t)=f(t)−λt$, so $g'(a)<0<g'(b)$. $g$ attains a minimum on $[a,b]$; the signs of $g'$ at the ends mean the minimum is not at $a$ or $b$. So it is interior and $g'(x)=0$.

Choose $M$ so that $f(β)=P(β)+M(β−α)^{n}$. Let $g(t)=f(t)−P(t)−M(t−α)^{n}$. Then $g(α)=g'(α)=⋯=g^{(n−1)}(α)=0$ and $g(β)=0$. Applying Rolle $n$ times gives $x$ with $g^{(n)}(x)=0$, i.e. $f^{(n)}(x)=n!M$.

items.prompt: Prove $|\sin x−\sin y|≤|x−y|$ for all real $x,y$.
If $f'(t)≠1$ for every real $t$, prove $f$ has at most one fixed point.
items.hint: Suppose two, apply MVT between them.
items.modelProof: If $f(a)=a$ and $f(b)=b$ with $a<b$, MVT gives $c$ with $f'(c)=\dfrac{b−a}{b−a}=1$.
$g'(x)=e^{x}−1$ is negative for $x<0$ and positive for $x>0$, so $g$ has its minimum $g(0)=0$.

items.prompt: If $f'>0$ on $(a,b)$, show $f$ is strictly increasing and its inverse $g$ satisfies $g'(f(x))=1/f'(x)$.
items.hint: MVT; then the difference quotient of $g$ is the reciprocal of that of $f$.
items.modelProof: MVT gives $f(y)−f(x)=f'(c)(y−x)>0$. For the inverse, $\dfrac{g(s)−g(y)}{s−y}=\dfrac{t−x}{f(t)−f(x)}$ with $s=f(t)$, $y=f(x)$; $g$ is continuous (B 5.6.5), so $t→x$ as $s→y$.

items.prompt: Compute $\lim_{x→0}\dfrac{1−\cos x}{x^{2}}$ and check that L'Hospital applies.

items.hint: Taylor with $n=4$: the cubic term vanishes.
items.modelProof: The degree-3 Taylor polynomial is $1−x^{2}/2$. Remainder $=\cos(c)x^{4}/24$, so the error is at most $0.1^{4}/24≈4.2×10^{−6}$.

items.prompt: If $f'(c)>0$, then $f$ is increasing on some interval around $c$.
items.explanation: $f(x)=x+2x^{2}\sin(1/x)$ at $c=0$. It is true if $f'$ is continuous at $c$.

items.prompt: If $f'(x)=0$ for all $x∈(a,b)$, then $f$ is constant on $(a,b)$.
If $f$ is differentiable on $ℝ$ and $f'$ is bounded, then $f$ is uniformly continuous.
A derivative can have a jump discontinuity.
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f$ is differentiable on $(0,∞)$ and $f(x)→L$ as $x→∞$, then $f'(x)→0$.

items.explanation: $f=x+\sin x$, $g=x$: $f/g→1$ but $f'/g'=1+\cos x$ has no limit. L'Hospital only goes one way.

lines: Apply the real MVT to $u$ and $v$: $u(b)−u(a)=(b−a)u'(c)$ and $v(b)−v(a)=(b−a)v'(c)$.
items.explanation: The two applications give two different points, $c_{1}$ for $u$ and $c_{2}$ for $v$. There is no single $c$ in general: $e^{ix}$ on $[0,2π]$.

lines: As $t→x$, the second factor tends to $f'(x)$.
As $t→x$, $f(t)→f(x)$, so the first factor tends to $g'(f(x))$.
items.explanation: $f(t)−f(x)$ can be 0 for $t$ arbitrarily close to $x$ (e.g. $f=x^{2}\sin(1/x)$ at 0), so the first factor is undefined. Rudin fixes this with remainder functions $u(t)$, $v(s)$ in 5.5; Bartle with Carathéodory's theorem 6.1.5.

lines: For $x≠0$, $f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)−\cos(1/x)$, which has no limit as $x→0$.
items.explanation: $f'(0)$ is defined by the difference quotient at 0, not by the limit of $f'(x)$. Here $|f(t)/t|≤|t|→0$, so $f'(0)=0$.

items.name: $x^{2}\sin(1/x)$, $f(0)=0$
items.details: Differentiable everywhere, $f'(0)=0$, but $f'$ is discontinuous at 0 (a second-kind discontinuity, as Darboux requires).

items.name: $x+2x^{2}\sin(1/x)$
items.details: $f'(0)=1>0$ yet $f$ is not increasing on any interval around 0.

items.name: $e^{ix}$ on $[0,2π]$
items.details: $f(2π)−f(0)=0$ but $|f'(x)|=1$ always: the MVT equation fails for complex functions (5.17).

items.name: $e^{−1/x^{2}}$, $f(0)=0$
items.details: Infinitely differentiable with every derivative 0 at 0, yet not 0 near 0. Taylor series need not represent the function.
